Because basically it's not the fuel that "explodes". It's the pressurized water and reactor structure that explodes, when the radioactivity gets out of control and produces too much heat. The radioactive material (and radioactive water) is pretty much unharmed, and continues to be highly radioactive.

A meltdown refers to those solid metal fuel rods melting. One fuel rod is safe to handle because it's a subcritical mass. The fission reaction just can't sustain itself. A whole lot of them close together creates a critical mass, where the fission reaction can keep cooking right along. When the water surrounding the rods boils off, the fuel rods are no longer being cooled, so the heat produced by that reaction starts heating the fuel rods more and more until they melt and pool on the floor. Now there's even less distance between the material, so the reaction just keeps running uncontrollably, irradiating everything nearby.
